BCG surveyed 1,500 workers and found the ones checking AI’s homework are more drained than the ones who skip the check entirely.

4 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by l ch on UnsplashEvery AI rollout comes with the same promise. Delegate the busywork, keep the judgment calls, watch your output climb. It sounds airtight. Offload the typing, keep the thinking.
New research out of Boston Consulting Group suggests that promise is backwards for a huge chunk of the workforce. The people spending their days reviewing, correcting, and second-guessing AI output aren’t the ones getting the cognitive break. They’re the ones burning out fastest.
BCG surveyed close to 1,500 full-time workers across industries and seniority levels in a study published in March 2026. Workers carrying a heavy AI-oversight load reported 14 percent more mental effort, 12 percent more mental fatigue, and 19 percent more information overload than workers whose AI engagement asked less supervision of them. The researchers gave the resulting state a name: AI brain fry.
If you spend your day reviewing pull requests an AI wrote, fact-checking a summary an AI generated, or auditing a dataset an AI cleaned, this probably doesn’t surprise you. It might be the first time someone put a number on it.
Why Checking Someone’s Work Is Harder Than Doing It
The intuitive model of AI assistance treats review as the lightweight half of the job. Writing code is hard. Reading code someone else wrote and deciding if it’s correct should be easier, right up until you remember how much of your own engineering training was spent learning to distrust code that looks right.
That’s the trap. AI output arrives with total confidence regardless of whether it deserves it. A hallucinated API call reads exactly like a correct one. A subtly wrong SQL join looks identical to a right one until you trace the data. The reviewer isn’t just checking for typos. They’re hunting for the one plausible-looking error buried inside a mountain of plausible-looking correctness, and they’re doing it without the benefit of having built the mental model that comes from writing the thing themselves.
Researchers studying AI-assisted software teams have described this as a distinct category of load, separate from the effort of building something from scratch. Evaluating and pruning a pile of AI-generated options, deciding which implementation fits your architecture, checking whether the “helpful” alternative the model offered actually breaks something downstream, all of that is its own tax, and it doesn’t show up on any velocity dashboard.
There’s also a switching cost that rarely gets counted. Reading code requires a different mental mode than writing it. Every time you move between generating and verifying, your brain has to tear down one framework and build another. Do that enough times in a day and the fatigue compounds even when the total volume of work looks manageable on paper.
The Tool Count Nobody’s Tracking
The BCG researchers found something else worth sitting with: productivity climbs when workers use one or two AI tools, still climbs a little with a third, and then reverses. Past three tools, output drops.
That threshold matters more than it looks. A lot of technical teams are stacking AI tools the same way they stacked SaaS subscriptions a decade ago, one for code generation, one for code review, one for documentation, one for testing, each with its own interface, its own failure modes, its own quirks to remember. Every tool you add isn’t just another capability. It’s another surface you have to supervise, and supervision is exactly the part of the job this research says is exhausting people.
This is a specific kind of irony. The pitch for adding tool number four is almost always “this will save you time.” The data says the fourth tool might be the one that starts costing you more time than it saves, once you count the oversight burden instead of just the raw output the tool produces on its own.
Delegation Isn’t the Same as Elimination
None of this means AI assistance is a net negative. Workers whose AI use required less active supervision, tools operating in narrower, more predictable domains, didn’t show the same fatigue signature. The exhaustion is specifically tied to oversight load, not AI use in general.
That distinction matters for how technical teams should actually be thinking about adoption. The question worth asking about a new AI tool isn’t “does this save time on the task.” It’s “does this save time on the task after accounting for how much verification the output demands.” A tool that writes code twice as fast but requires line-by-line scrutiny might be a wash, or worse, once you price in the reviewer’s attention as a finite resource instead of a free one.
That reframing runs against almost every vendor pitch in the market right now, which sell speed of generation and stay quiet about cost of verification. It’s also the reason this study is landing hard with technical audiences. Anyone who has spent an afternoon debugging a bug an AI assistant introduced with total confidence already knew this in their body. BCG just gave it a number.
What This Actually Changes
The practical takeaway isn’t to abandon AI tools. It’s to stop measuring their value purely by what they produce and start measuring it by what they demand from the human checking the output. A tool that hands you a clean, narrow, low-variance result earns its place. A tool that hands you a firehose of plausible-sounding options and calls that a feature is quietly transferring its workload onto your attention span instead of eliminating it.
The next wave of AI tooling that actually earns adoption from technical teams probably won’t be the one that generates the most. It’ll be the one that generates the least you have to check.
